terms.gloss: tend towards, be heading for (of how things are going)
terms.grammar: phrase: rēs as the subject, ad with the accusative
evidence: Liv. 1.9.6: ad vim spectāre rēs coepit (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Fam. 14.5.1: ad arma rem spectāre (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Latin says where things are heading rather than naming a trend. The verb’s first sense is “look at, watch”; Lewis & Short gives this sense as “to tend, incline, refer”.

terms.gloss: a turn, a shift (of the times); a tendency
evidence: Cic. Fam. 6.10.5: inclīnātiōnēs temporum atque momenta (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Literally a leaning, a bending. Lewis & Short: figuratively an inclination or tendency (ad meliōrem spem, Cic. Sest. 67), a bias or favour, and a change in the times. Traupman’s word for “trend”. For a trend in fashion, see style.

phrases.english: things began to head towards violence

phrases.latin: nisi forte rēbus cūnctīs inest quīdam velut orbis, ut quem ad modum temporum vicēs ita mōrum vertantur
phrases.english: unless perhaps there is a kind of cycle in all things, so that ways of life change as the seasons do

sources: Lewis & Short: specto · Lewis & Short: inclinatio
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 397, checked against the searchable text of the book (11 November 2026).
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-tacitus), checked against the editions named there.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
